idiom_name: Jakarta Messaging Message (header fields + properties + body subinterfaces)
implementation_notes: Jakarta Messaging (JMS) is the canonical library realization: the Message interface is the root of every message and carries the standard header fields (JMSMessageID, JMSDestination, JMSCorrelationID, JMSExpiration, JMSPriority, JMSRedelivered, JMSTimestamp, JMSType) plus arbitrary application properties, while the body lives in the subinterfaces - TextMessage (setText), BytesMessage, MapMessage, StreamMessage, ObjectMessage - so providers route on header fields without reading the body. For HTTP-shaped boundaries java.net.http.HttpRequest pairs headers (HttpHeaders) with a BodyPublisher body, and Jakarta Mail's MimeMessage is the mail form of the same split. Hand-writing an envelope class (or a record with headers plus payload) remains justified for a custom wire format or when the broker client library defines its own message type.
pitfalls: Property names are untyped strings, so a typo fails only at runtime - and a message selector referring to a name nobody set silently matches nothing.

ObjectMessage serializes the body with Java native serialization: it only works when producer and consumer share class definitions and is unsafe for untrusted payloads, which is why it is a poor integration format.

Some header fields are provider-managed (setting JMSMessageID is ignored or rejected, JMSRedelivered is set by the provider), and JMSCorrelationID accepts both provider-generated and application-chosen values - mixing the two breaks correlation.
